Bohk-Ewald and Rau model of age-specific rates of mortality improvement

Source: R/model-bohk_rau.R
bohk_rau.Rd

The probabilistic model of Bohk-Ewald and Rau (2017) forecasts rates of mortality improvement (ROMIs) by age, whose trends over time differ between ages, so that the age pattern of mortality decline changes over the forecast. For each age x and year t the ROMI is

Usage

bohk_rau(
  core = c("exponential", "linear"),
  limits = c(0.005, 0.035),
  smooth = TRUE,
  draws = c("quantiles", "samples"),
  mcmc = c(chains = 5, iterations = 5200, burn_in = 200, thin = 5)
)

Arguments

core

"exponential" or "linear" core model.

limits

Lower and upper limit of the forecast ROMIs, or NULL for none.

smooth

Smooth the death rates with two-dimensional P-splines before computing the ROMIs (FALSE: the observed rates, with 0.5 deaths in cells without deaths, for example when the rates were smoothed in a preprocessing step).

draws

"quantiles" (equation 20 of the paper) or "samples".

mcmc

Settings of the sampler, a named vector: chains, iterations per chain (burn-in included), burn_in and thin. Elements left out keep their defaults.

Value

A model specification.

Details

rho[x, t] = 1 - m[x, t + 1] / m[x, t]

(equation 1 of the paper; positive when mortality falls), computed from death rates smoothed over age and time with two-dimensional P-splines (Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004). One of two Bayesian core models describes the ROMIs of every age over the years of the base period:

  • core = "exponential" (the core model of the paper's applications): rho[x, t] ~ N(exp(b1[x] + b2[x] log t), sigma^2), b1[x] ~ N(theta1[x], sigma1^2), b2[x] ~ N(theta2[x], sigma2^2), with theta1[x] and theta2[x] the least-squares estimates of log rho[x, t] = theta1[x] + theta2[x] log t for each age and sigma, sigma1, sigma2 uniform on (0, 1). Improvements can level off; mortality increases cannot be forecast.

  • core = "linear": rho[x, t] ~ N(b1[x] + b2[x] t, sigma^2) with (b1[x], b2[x]) bivariate normal with means mu1, mu2 and covariance from standard deviations omega1, omega2 and correlation r; uniform priors sigma, omega1, omega2 on (0, 1), mu1, mu2 on (-0.1, 0.1) and r on (-1, 1). Trends of the improvements continue linearly.

The posterior and the future ROMIs (each one the curve of a posterior sample plus normal noise with that sample's sigma) are sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo. Forecast ROMIs outside limits are set to the nearest limit (the paper uses 0.005 and 0.035: mortality declines by at least 0.5% and at most 3.5% a year; it excludes implausible forecasts "by setting thresholds", which this package reads as setting the values to the thresholds). Death rates follow from the last smoothed rates of the base period by m[x, t] = m[x, t - 1] (1 - rho[x, t - 1]) (equation 20). With draws = "quantiles" (the paper's method) draw j of n applies the quantile (j - 0.5) / n of the forecast ROMIs at every age and year, so that the draws give the quantiles of the death rates as in the paper. These draws are comonotone across ages and years; their order is permuted at random, so that the draws of different strata are independent. With draws = "samples" (package-specific) every draw is the path of one posterior sample with its own noise. Such paths give much narrower intervals of summary measures such as life expectancy, because the yearly noise of the improvements averages out over ages and years.

The defaults follow the paper's application (its Table 3): the exponential core model, five chains of 5,200 iterations with the first 200 discarded and every fifth kept (5,000 samples), and the limits 0.005 and 0.035. The paper recommends a base period at least as long as the forecast horizon, and uses single years of age from 0.

What differs from the paper. The paper samples with JAGS; here a sampler written for this package is used (Metropolis steps for the curve parameters of each age, with proposals scaled by the curvature at the least-squares estimates and adapted during the burn-in; conjugate draws of the variances truncated to the prior range; moves that scale sigma1 or sigma2 together with the deviations of the curve parameters from theta; Gibbs and slice sampling steps for the linear core model). The paper does not state the following, which are choices of this package (package-specific, reference unknown):

  • time t counts the years of the base period from 1 (the change from the first to the second year) and continues into the forecast;

  • ROMIs below the lower limit (0.001 with limits = NULL or a lower limit of 0 or below) are set to that limit in the least-squares fit of theta (the paper sets negative values "to a minimum that is greater than zero");

  • the P-spline surface has cubic B-splines with knots every 5 years of age and time and second-order penalties, with both smoothing parameters chosen by BIC (the paper uses the package MortalitySmooth); when the grid starts with age 0 as its own interval, the rates of age 0 are smoothed over time only (as mt_smooth() leaves out the first year of life);

  • forecast ROMIs are kept below 1 so that rates stay positive.

The model's option to let a population converge to the mortality trend of reference populations, by weights that shift from the population to the references over the forecast years, is not implemented: the paper leaves the weighting scheme open. Each stratum is forecast from its own data.

Draws describe the expected (smoothed) rates; predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates. Fitted rates are the smoothed rates (the observed rates with smooth = FALSE). The Gelman-Rubin statistics of the scalar parameters and the largest one of the curve parameters are reported by mt_parameters() (rhat); values above 1.1 give a warning. With the default settings a fit takes about 6 seconds per stratum for 71 ages and 36 years.

References

Bohk-Ewald C, Rau R (2017). Probabilistic mortality forecasting with varying age-specific survival improvements. Genus 73(1): 1. doi:10.1186/s41118-016-0017-8

Currie ID, Durban M, Eilers PHC (2004). Smoothing and forecasting mortality rates. Statistical Modelling 4(4): 279-298.

Examples

x <- mt_subset(mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019), sex == "female")
# shorter chains than the defaults of the paper, for a quick example
spec <- bohk_rau(mcmc = c(chains = 2, iterations = 3200, burn_in = 200, thin = 3))
set.seed(1)
fit <- mt_fit(spec, x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
life_expectancy(fc)
